name: Dolores Huerta
role: Labor leader and civil rights activist, co-founder of the United Farm Workers (1930–2026)
summary: American farmworker organizer who co-founded the National Farm Workers Association and the United Farm Workers, lobbied for the 1986 immigrant legalization and California farm labor law, and later became a vocal feminist and LGBT-rights advocate. She holds a committed, progressive-Democratic outlook built on grassroots organizing, nonviolence and coalition work between labor, immigrant, women's and environmental movements.

abortion-legal.rationale: Says abortion is a right women have and need, because a woman must control her own body to control her life; she changed from her Catholic upbringing and has held this since.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Describes the union's first contracts and the right to organize as what won farmworkers their benefits, and wants that right extended nationally.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Backs teaching the omitted history of Latinos, Black Americans and Native Americans and sued a school district over racially skewed expulsions.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Testified that it was wrong to discriminate by sexual orientation and calls gay and lesbian rights basic human rights, which rejects criminalizing same-sex relations.

direct-action.rationale: Says voting is the ultimate way to change things and pairs protest with winning elections and school boards and city councils, not replacing them.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: States that everybody has rights and defines feminism as believing all are equal with no racism, sexism or homophobia.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Argues that labor, immigrant, environmental and LGBT movements must work together and cannot win in silos, and calls racism and misogyny together a call to action.

means-match-ends.rationale: Holds that nonviolent methods carry a spiritual power and that campaigners should not come to hate opponents but bring love instead of hatred.

minority-language-support.rationale: Lists getting ballots printed in Spanish among the laws she helped pass.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Her organizing method trains ordinary people to run the issues in their own communities and says people must take the power and make changes themselves.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Describes a macho sexist culture and says civil rights movements fought for their people but not their women.

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: Says that anyone who turns to violence is joining the other side, and tells protesters to answer violence with nonviolence.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Said that instead of pulling statues down they should be moved to a museum once city councils are won.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: Names the racism of employers as the reason farmworkers lack basic rights and says racism and bigotry must still be addressed across the country.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Said whom one marries is a constitutional right of privacy and that anyone unsupportive of gay and lesbian rights is against human rights; she lobbied the legislature on the marriage equality bill.

single-official-language.rationale: Lists Spanish-language ballots among her achievements, which contradicts making one language the sole language of public life.

unions-good.rationale: Co-founded the farmworkers' union and says everyone has to support labor unions alongside the other movements.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Said she was for the public option and single payer in the 2010 health-reform fight.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Counts among her wins the removal of citizenship requirements for public assistance and a law giving legal immigrants public assistance.

notes: Written from her own interviews and speeches. Themes searched: economy and labor, immigration, women's and LGBT rights, race, violence and protest, electoral politics, environment, world affairs. Died 2026-10-28. Government (courts, executive power, federalism) and world (wars, alliances, UN) have no stated positions found, so those stay null; positions where she only endorsed a candidate, or where the evidence was a news report of her words, were not used. Her pre-1960s opposition to abortion and contraception was replaced by an explicit, sustained pro-choice position that she has held for decades, so the later position is answered.
